opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the final round mattered less than people might assume. By the time you reach that stage, the team has usually already seen a lot: your past work, your code, what you've built. In my case I think the open-source work I'd done, especially on reinforcement learning infrastructure, carried a lot of weight before I even walked into the room. It showed I could actually ship things that other people use, not just talk about ideas.

That said, the final round still has to confirm that impression. What I tried to do was simply be myself: think out loud, be honest when I didn't know something, and show how I approach a problem I haven't seen before. I think interviewers care a lot about whether you can work through ambiguity and whether they'd enjoy debugging something with you at two in the morning. If you try too hard to perform or pretend to know everything, it usually backfires.

So my answer is that the interview was more like the last checkbox. It confirmed what my track record already suggested. If I have advice for people, it's to put your energy into building real things beforehand, because that does most of the talking for you. Then in the interview, just stay calm and communicate clearly.

r001.rationale: The response says the final round confirmed an impression and was the “last checkbox”; it attributes most of the weight to prior open-source work. It does not clearly say Jiayi was hired because his interview performance demonstrated practical engineering ability.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the final round mattered less for what I said and more for how I handled not knowing things. There was one question about scaling a training system where I genuinely didn't have a clean answer. Instead of bluffing, I walked through how I'd reason about it, said where I was uncertain, and asked a couple of clarifying questions back. Later I heard that was the part that stood out.

The other thing was that I'd actually built stuff I could talk about in detail. When they asked about my open source work, I could go deep on design decisions, tradeoffs I regretted, bugs that took me days. That's hard to fake, and I think it signaled that I'd ship real things rather than just talk about them.

So if I had to put a number on it, I'd say the interview maybe confirmed what my track record already suggested. It didn't win the job on its own, but a bad one could have definitely lost it.

r001.rationale: He says discussing concrete open-source work, including design tradeoffs and difficult bugs, showed he could ship real things; he describes the interview as confirming his track record.

astra-6.text: I think my performance in the final round helped them see how I think and how I would work with the team. I tried to explain my reasoning clearly and be honest about what I knew and what I still needed to learn. I can’t know exactly what tipped the decision, but I hope I showed that I was engaged, willing to learn, and someone they could work well with.

r001.rationale: The response says the interview showed how Jiayi thinks and works with a team, but does not say it demonstrated practical engineering ability.
